Suggested initial draft for review:

Problem (one sentence): Decision-makers lack a concise, evidence-based account of the current state, key drivers, and practical policy/operational options for [project topic], which prevents timely, low-cost actions and reliable monitoring of outcomes. 

Focused research questions (3–4): (1) What is the current baseline and most robust indicators we can measure quickly?; (2) Which candidate drivers correlate with or plausibly explain the baseline variation given available data?; (3) Which 2–3 actionable interventions/options are feasible within the sponsor’s constraints and what is their expected direction/magnitude of effect (qualitative + simple quantitative scenarios)?; (4) How should success be monitored with a minimal ongoing data plan?

High-level work packages (4) and major tasks: WP1 — Rapid evidence & data audit: inventory sources, assess quality, extract core indicators; WP2 — Targeted analysis: descriptive baseline, simple multivariate checks / sensitivity analyses, short scenario modeling for top options; WP3 — Options appraisal & recommendations: synthesize evidence, rank options by impact/feasibility/risk, draft implementation notes; WP4 — Communication & monitoring: produce one-page brief + 5-slide deck for non‑technical stakeholders and a 3‑metric monitoring dashboard (template). Each WP is designed to be parallelizable across three researchers + part-time analyst with minimal handoffs (audit → analysis → synthesis → comms).

Tangible benefits: WP1–WP3 produce decision-ready artifacts (baseline snapshot, ranked options with supporting evidence, short implementation notes) that map directly to sponsor needs; WP4 translates these into stakeholder-ready deliverables and a simple monitoring plan to track early outcomes. 

Success criteria & tracking (brief): delivery of the four artifacts above, reproducible data inventory + analysis scripts, sponsor sign-off on the brief, and weekly 30‑minute standups plus two milestone reviews (midpoint and final) to track progress; I’ll present this draft in tomorrow’s coordination call for rapid iteration.

Problem (2 sentences): The sponsor faces elevated operational and reputational risk from AI‑assisted decision tools over the next 12–18 months because governance and controls vary across units and a recent set of incidents/near‑misses show recurring failure modes that could escalate if unaddressed. This project will identify 2–3 near‑term, high‑impact, low‑cost interventions the sponsor can adopt within 12–18 months and define simple monitoring metrics to track early effects.  

Focused research questions (one sentence): Q1) What is the current baseline of AI use, control gaps, and the most credible failure modes in scope?; Q2) Which failure modes and contextual factors appear most responsible for recent incidents/near‑misses in the curated dataset?; Q3) Which 2–3 interventions are feasible within the sponsor’s operational constraints and likely to reduce those risks (qualitative ranking + simple scenario estimates)?; Q4) What minimal monitoring metrics and data sources will show early signals that interventions are working?  

Work packages (one sentence, each mapped to questions): WP1 — Rapid audit (Q1): inventory AI uses from the landscape report, classify tool types and governance gaps, and extract/clean indicators from the incident dataset; WP2 — Incident analysis & failure‑mode mapping (Q2): code incidents by root cause, quantify frequency/severity patterns, and surface high‑leverage failure modes; WP3 — Intervention appraisal & simple scenarios (Q3): generate 4–6 candidate interventions, do quick feasibility checks with operational owners, and produce a ranked short list with qualitative + bounded quantitative scenario estimates; WP4 — Decision package & monitoring plan (Q4): produce a one‑page executive brief, 5‑slide decision deck, implementation notes for each recommended intervention (roles, quick wins, risks), and a 3‑metric monitoring dashboard template.  

Team fit and sequencing (one sentence): The four WPs contain separable 2–3 day tasks suitable for three researchers plus a part‑time analyst (1 day/week), avoid complex modeling or new data collection, are parallelizable (audit → analysis → appraisal → comms with minimal handoffs), and produce decision‑ready artifacts the sponsor can act on.

Problem: The sponsor faces near‑term operational and reputational risk from unevenly governed AI‑assisted decision tools—recent incidents and near‑misses reveal recurring failure modes and inconsistent controls across business units; this project will identify 2–3 near‑term (12–18 month), low‑cost interventions to reduce those risks and define simple metrics to monitor early effects.  

Research questions: Q1) What is the baseline of AI use, governance gaps, and the top failure modes across units?; Q2) Which failure modes in the curated incident dataset drive the greatest near‑term operational/reputational risk?; Q3) Which 2–3 interventions are feasible within the sponsor’s constraints and likely to reduce those risks (ranked by impact, cost, speed)?; Q4) What 3 straightforward monitoring metrics and data sources will show early signals that interventions are working?  

Work packages (outputs, 1–3 day sprint notes, analyst need): WP1 — Rapid audit (Q1): tasks—(a) extract and tabulate AI uses and governance gaps from the landscape report (researcher 1–2 days per unit), (b) pull/clean key incident fields from the curated dataset (analyst support recommended for 1–2 days once available); deliverable—inventory spreadsheet + 5–7 baseline indicators. WP2 — Incident analysis & failure‑mode mapping (Q2): tasks—(a) rapid coding of a prioritized sample of incidents to identify root causes (researcher can code 20–50 cases in 2–3 days), (b) aggregate frequency/severity counts (analyst helpful but not required for initial counts); deliverable—failure‑mode brief with top 3 risks and representative examples. WP3 — Intervention appraisal & quick scenarios (Q3): tasks—(a) generate 4–6 candidate interventions from evidence and constraints (researcher 1–2 days), (b) one‑day feasibility calls with 2–3 operational owners, (c) produce simple bounded scenarios (researcher; analyst can add numeric examples when back); deliverable—ranked short list (2–3 recommended) with implementation notes. WP4 — Decision package & monitoring plan (Q4): tasks—(a) produce one‑page executive brief + 5‑slide deck (researcher 1–2 days), (b) define a 3‑metric monitoring dashboard template and list data owners (researcher; analyst to populate sample values when available); deliverable—executive decision package and dashboard template ready for sponsor review.  

Early deliverables and sequencing: within the first 1–2 weeks the team can credibly deliver (i) the inventory + cleaned incident extract sample, (ii) a 1‑page failure‑mode snapshot, and (iii) a draft one‑page decision brief; sequencing is audit → incident coding → intervention appraisal → final decision package, with tasks parallelizable across three researchers to accommodate the analyst’s two‑day absence.  

Success criteria & progress tracking: (1) What success looks like — sponsor selects and commits to 1–2 prioritized interventions for near‑term rollout and accepts the 3‑metric dashboard as the monitoring approach, with documented mitigation steps or reduced incident signals within 6–12 months; (2) Interim milestones — Week 1: inventory + cleaned incident extract (deliverable); Week 2: failure‑mode snapshot + initial intervention ideas (deliverable); Week 3–4: ranked interventions, feasibility notes, and monitoring template (deliverable); (3) Simple indicators and governance — monitor three agreed metrics via the dashboard (sample values from the incident extract), hold weekly 30‑minute standups and a mid‑project review after WP2, and provide the sponsor with inventory, incident coding file, analysis notes, the one‑page brief, and a 5‑slide deck as the record of decisions and evidence.

rounds.response:
Problem & questions: Leaders face near‑term operational and reputational risk because AI‑assisted decision tools are deployed unevenly across units and recent incidents show recurring failures; we are answering (1) what tools and control gaps exist, (2) which failure modes drive most risk, (3) which 2–3 near‑term fixes are feasible and impactful, and (4) how to measure early success.  

What we see now: in a hand‑coded ~1/3 sample most incidents cluster on late or missing escalation and unclear ownership, and many lack sufficient logging to support fast investigation; deployment/configuration errors and outright incorrect outputs form a smaller cluster; these are early but defensible signals supported by the analyst’s cleaned timestamps and baseline rates, with full coding to follow.  

Immediate proposals & Day‑10 deliverables: implement (a) a human sign‑off gate for defined high‑risk outputs, (b) a rapid incident triage process plus weekly playbook review to assign owners and fixes, and (c) a deployment checklist with staged rollouts, required logging, and rollback criteria — by Day‑10 we will deliver a risk snapshot, a ranked 2–3 item intervention short list (with owners), and a sample 3‑metric dashboard (Incident count; Median time‑to‑detection; Severity‑weighted score).  

What comes after Day‑10 & success criteria: complete full incident coding, refine metric thresholds and baselines, pilot the top intervention(s) in one unit, and finalize the success‑criteria document; success will be judged by sponsor selection of interventions plus early signal movement — fewer incidents, faster detection (median <24 hours), and a reduction in high‑severity events.  

CEO one‑pager (5 bullets you can paste): • Core risk: uneven AI controls create operational and reputational exposure; • Early learning: in our sampled incidents most problems stem from late escalation and poor logging (early signal based on ~1/3 sample); • What we propose now: human sign‑off for high‑risk outputs; rapid triage + weekly playbook; deployment checklist + logging/rollback; • What we’ll do next: finish full coding, refine metrics, pilot selected fixes, finalize rollout plan; • How we’ll know it’s working: incident counts fall, detection speeds up, and high‑severity events decline.
